_link.title: I can use the arrow convention to represent magnetic fields going into or out of the page

toLevel2.question: What symbol represents a magnetic field directed into the page?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A cross represents the tail feathers of an arrow moving away from you, indicating the field is directed into the page.

distractors.answer: A dot (•)
distractors.explanation: A dot represents a field coming out of the page toward you, like the tip of an approaching arrow.

distractors.answer: A horizontal line (—)
distractors.explanation: A horizontal line is not used to represent field direction into or out of the page.

distractors.answer: A circle (○)
distractors.explanation: An empty circle is not the standard symbol for field direction into the page.

toLevel2.question: What symbol represents a magnetic field directed out of the page?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A dot represents the tip of an arrow coming toward you, indicating the field is directed out of the page.

distractors.answer: A cross (✕)
distractors.explanation: A cross represents a field going into the page, not out of it.

distractors.answer: A triangle (△)
distractors.explanation: A triangle is not the standard symbol used for magnetic field direction.

distractors.answer: A square (□)
distractors.explanation: A square is not used to represent magnetic field direction into or out of the page.

toLevel2.question: The cross symbol for a field into the page represents which part of an arrow?
toLevel2.correct: The tail feathers seen from behind as the arrow moves away
toLevel2.correctExplanation: When an arrow flies away from you, you see the crossed tail feathers from behind, giving the ✕ symbol.

distractors.answer: The sharp tip of the arrow coming toward you from the front
distractors.explanation: The tip coming toward you is represented by a dot, not a cross.

distractors.answer: The middle shaft of the arrow viewed from the side position
distractors.explanation: The side view of an arrow is a line, not a cross; the cross is the tail seen from behind.

distractors.answer: The bow string that launches the arrow forward from behind
distractors.explanation: The bowstring is not part of the arrow convention for field direction.

toLevel2.question: A diagram shows a region filled with dots (•). In which direction is the magnetic field?
toLevel2.correct: Out of the page, toward the viewer
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Dots represent the tip of an arrow pointing toward you, so the field is directed out of the page.

distractors.answer: Into the page, away from the viewer
distractors.explanation: A field into the page is shown by crosses, not dots.

distractors.answer: To the right across the page surface
distractors.explanation: Dots indicate a field perpendicular to the page, not along the page surface.

distractors.answer: Downward along the page from top to bottom
distractors.explanation: Dots represent a field perpendicular to the page, not along it.

toLevel2.question: Why is the arrow convention used in physics diagrams?
toLevel2.correct: To show three-dimensional field directions on a flat two-dimensional page
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Physics problems often involve fields perpendicular to the page that cannot be shown with ordinary arrows; the dot and cross convention solves this.

distractors.answer: To make diagrams more colourful and visually appealing for students
distractors.explanation: The convention is functional, not decorative; it conveys essential directional information.

distractors.answer: To hide the actual field direction from students during exams
distractors.explanation: The convention reveals field direction clearly; it does not hide information.

distractors.answer: To indicate which parts of the diagram have zero magnetic field
distractors.explanation: Dots and crosses indicate where the field exists and its direction, not where it is zero.

toLevel2.question: A cross (✕) represents a magnetic field coming out of the page toward the viewer.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A cross represents a field going into the page (away from the viewer). A dot represents a field coming out of the page.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Students commonly confuse dots and crosses; the cross is the tail of an arrow going away, meaning into the page.

toLevel2.question: The dot and cross convention can also be used to represent the direction of current flow into or out of the page.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The same convention applies to any vector direction: current, velocity, or force can all use dots and crosses for perpendicular-to-page directions.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may think the convention only applies to magnetic fields, but it is a general convention for any vector direction.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about the arrow convention.
toLevel2.sentence: A {{blank:1}} represents a field going into the page, while a {{blank:2}} represents a field coming out of the page.

1.correctExplanation: A cross (✕) shows the tail feathers of an arrow moving away, indicating the field goes into the page.

distractors.answer: dot
distractors.explanation: A dot shows the tip of an approaching arrow, meaning the field comes out of the page.

distractors.answer: circle
distractors.explanation: An empty circle is not the standard symbol for field direction.

2.correctExplanation: A dot (•) shows the tip of an arrow coming toward you, indicating the field comes out of the page.

distractors.answer: cross
distractors.explanation: A cross shows the field going into the page, not out of it.

distractors.answer: square
distractors.explanation: A square is not part of the standard arrow convention for field direction.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about the analogy.
toLevel2.sentence: The cross symbol is like seeing the {{blank:1}} of an arrow flying away from you into the page.

1.correctExplanation: When an arrow moves away, you see its tail feathers from behind, which form a cross pattern.

distractors.answer: pointed tip
distractors.explanation: The pointed tip is what you see when the arrow comes toward you, represented by a dot.

distractors.answer: wooden shaft
distractors.explanation: The shaft viewed from behind would appear as a dot, not a cross.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about using the convention.
toLevel2.sentence: The dot and cross convention allows {{blank:1}} field directions to be shown on a two-dimensional page.

1.correctExplanation: The convention represents the third dimension (into/out of the page) that cannot be shown with ordinary in-plane arrows.

distractors.answer: two-dimensional
distractors.explanation: Two-dimensional directions can be shown with ordinary arrows; the convention addresses the third dimension.

distractors.answer: one-dimensional
distractors.explanation: The convention addresses multi-dimensional representation, not just one dimension.

toLevel3.question: Why is it important to distinguish between a field going into and out of the page when solving force problems?
toLevel3.correct: The direction of the force depends on the field direction through the right-hand rules
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The right-hand slap rule requires knowing the exact field direction to determine the force direction; reversing the field reverses the force.

distractors.answer: It does not matter because the force is always the same regardless of field direction
distractors.explanation: Force direction depends critically on field direction; reversing the field reverses the force.

distractors.answer: The distinction only affects the magnitude of the force, not its direction
distractors.explanation: The field direction affects the force direction through the cross product, not just the magnitude.

distractors.answer: It matters only for electric fields, not for magnetic fields at all
distractors.explanation: The convention is essential for magnetic field problems involving force on charges and currents.

toLevel3.question: A wire carries current to the right across the page. The magnetic field is represented by crosses filling the region. What can you conclude about the field direction relative to the current?
toLevel3.correct: The field is perpendicular to the current, directed into the page
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The current flows in the plane of the page (to the right) while the crosses indicate the field goes into the page, making them perpendicular.

distractors.answer: The field is parallel to the current, both going to the right
distractors.explanation: Crosses indicate the field goes into the page, not along the page; the field is perpendicular to the current.

distractors.answer: The field is opposite to the current, going to the left side
distractors.explanation: The crosses show the field goes into the page, not to the left along the page surface.

distractors.answer: The field direction cannot be determined from the crosses shown
distractors.explanation: Crosses unambiguously indicate a field directed into the page.

toLevel3.question: How does the arrow convention relate to the mnemonic of a real arrow flying through space?
toLevel3.correct: A dot looks like the arrow tip approaching you; a cross looks like the tail feathers receding
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The analogy connects the 2D symbol to a 3D arrow: the dot is the point of an approaching arrow, the cross is the fletching of a departing one.

distractors.answer: A dot represents the arrow's shadow on the ground while the cross represents its height
distractors.explanation: The analogy is about viewing the arrow head-on versus from behind, not about shadows.

distractors.answer: A dot is used for slow arrows and a cross is used for fast arrows only
distractors.explanation: Speed is irrelevant; the symbols indicate direction of the field, not its magnitude.

distractors.answer: A dot represents a broken arrow and a cross represents a whole arrow fully
distractors.explanation: The symbols represent viewing angle (front vs rear), not the condition of the arrow.

toLevel3.question: In a diagram, an electron moves upward through a region of crosses. What do the crosses tell you about the problem setup?
toLevel3.correct: The magnetic field is directed into the page while the electron moves in the plane of the page
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Crosses indicate the field is into the page. The electron moves upward within the page. The field and velocity are perpendicular.

distractors.answer: The electron is moving into the page along with the magnetic field shown
distractors.explanation: The electron is described as moving upward (in the page plane); the crosses show the field direction, not the electron's.

distractors.answer: The crosses indicate that no magnetic field exists in that particular region
distractors.explanation: Crosses specifically indicate a field is present and directed into the page.

distractors.answer: The magnetic field and electron are both moving out of the page together
distractors.explanation: Crosses indicate the field is into the page, and the electron moves upward in the page plane.

toLevel3.question: A student draws dots on the left half of a diagram and crosses on the right half. What does this represent?
toLevel3.correct: The field comes out of the page on the left and goes into the page on the right
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Dots show the field emerging from the page on the left, while crosses show it going into the page on the right, indicating the field changes direction.

distractors.answer: The field is stronger on the left side and weaker on the right side
distractors.explanation: Dots and crosses indicate direction, not strength; strength would be shown by symbol density.

distractors.answer: There is no magnetic field present in either half of the diagram shown
distractors.explanation: Both dots and crosses indicate the presence of a magnetic field with specific directions.

distractors.answer: The magnetic field is horizontal, pointing from left to right across the page
distractors.explanation: Dots and crosses indicate perpendicular-to-page directions, not in-plane horizontal directions.

toLevel3.question: Why can the same dot and cross convention be used for current direction, velocity, and force as well as magnetic field?
toLevel3.correct: All are vector quantities that may need to be shown perpendicular to the page
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The convention is a general tool for representing any vector pointing into or out of the page, not specific to magnetic fields alone.

distractors.answer: Because current, velocity, and force are all the same physical quantity
distractors.explanation: These are different physical quantities; they share the convention because all are vectors.

distractors.answer: The convention can only be used for magnetic fields and nothing else at all
distractors.explanation: The convention applies to any vector that needs to be shown perpendicular to the page.

distractors.answer: Because all vectors always point into the page and never out of it
distractors.explanation: Vectors can point in any direction; dots show out-of-page and crosses show into-page.

toLevel3.question: If the density of crosses in a diagram is higher in one region, the magnetic field is stronger there.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: More densely packed crosses indicate a stronger field going into the page, just as closely spaced field lines indicate stronger fields.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may think all crosses represent the same strength, but symbol density can indicate field strength in diagrams.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about the arrow convention in problems.
toLevel3.sentence: When applying the right-hand slap rule, knowing whether the field is into the page ({{blank:1}}) or out of the page ({{blank:2}}) determines the direction of the force.

1.correctExplanation: Crosses indicate the field is directed into the page, which is needed as an input for the right-hand slap rule.

distractors.answer: dots
distractors.explanation: Dots indicate the field is out of the page, not into it.

distractors.answer: arrows
distractors.explanation: Arrows pointing into the page would work but the conventional symbol is a cross.

2.correctExplanation: Dots indicate the field is directed out of the page toward the viewer.

distractors.answer: crosses
distractors.explanation: Crosses indicate the field going into the page, not out of it.

distractors.answer: dashes
distractors.explanation: Dashes are not the standard symbol for out-of-page field direction.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about interpreting diagrams.
toLevel3.sentence: An electron moving to the right through a field shown by crosses is moving {{blank:1}} to the magnetic field.

1.correctExplanation: The electron moves in the plane of the page while the field goes into the page, making them perpendicular.

distractors.answer: parallel
distractors.explanation: The electron moves in the page plane while the field is perpendicular to the page; they are not parallel.

distractors.answer: opposite
distractors.explanation: Opposite implies antiparallel; the electron's motion and field are at 90°, not 180°.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about the convention's purpose.
toLevel3.sentence: The dot and cross convention is necessary because many physics problems involve fields that are {{blank:1}} to the page surface.

1.correctExplanation: Fields perpendicular to the page cannot be shown with ordinary in-plane arrows, requiring the dot and cross convention.

distractors.answer: parallel
distractors.explanation: Fields parallel to the page can be shown with ordinary arrows; the convention is for perpendicular fields.

distractors.answer: tangential
distractors.explanation: Tangential fields lie along the page surface and can be shown with arrows; perpendicular ones need dots and crosses.

toLevel4.question: An electron moves to the right through a region of dots. Using the right-hand slap rule, in which direction is the magnetic force on the electron?
toLevel4.correct: Downward (toward the bottom of the page)
toLevel4.correctExplanation: For a positive charge moving right in a field out of the page: thumb right, fingers out of page, palm pushes up. Since the electron is negative, the actual force is downward.

distractors.answer: Upward (toward the top of the page)
distractors.explanation: Upward is the result for a positive charge; the electron's negative charge reverses the force to downward.

distractors.answer: Into the page alongside the field direction
distractors.explanation: The force is perpendicular to both velocity and field, not along either of them.

distractors.answer: To the left, opposite to the electron's motion
distractors.explanation: Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, not opposite to it; this would be a braking force.

toLevel4.question: A wire carries current to the left across the page in a field represented by crosses. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
toLevel4.correct: Downward (toward the bottom of the page)
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Right-hand slap: thumb points left (current), fingers point into page (crosses). Palm faces downward, so force is downward.

distractors.answer: Upward (toward the top of the page)
distractors.explanation: Upward would result if the current were to the right; with current to the left, the force reverses to downward.

distractors.answer: Out of the page toward the viewer directly
distractors.explanation: The force is in the plane of the page, perpendicular to both current and field.

distractors.answer: To the right, opposite to the current direction
distractors.explanation: Magnetic force is perpendicular to the current, not opposite to it.

toLevel4.question: A proton enters a region of crosses moving upward. What path will the proton follow?
toLevel4.correct: It will curve to the right in a circular arc
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Right-hand slap: thumb up (velocity), fingers into page (crosses), palm faces right. The force deflects the proton to the right, creating circular motion.

distractors.answer: It will curve to the left in a circular arc
distractors.explanation: Left would be correct for a negative charge; the proton is positive so it curves right.

distractors.answer: It will continue straight upward without deflecting
distractors.explanation: The magnetic force acts perpendicular to the velocity, causing the path to curve.

distractors.answer: It will slow down and come to a stop in the field
distractors.explanation: Magnetic force does no work; it changes direction but not speed, so the proton never stops.

toLevel4.question: Two parallel wires are drawn on a page. Wire A carries current into the page (shown by a cross). Wire B carries current out of the page (shown by a dot). What can you determine about the direction of the force between them?
toLevel4.correct: The wires repel each other because they carry current in opposite directions
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Parallel wires with currents in opposite directions repel; the cross and dot confirm the currents are antiparallel.

distractors.answer: The wires attract because one has a cross and the other has a dot
distractors.explanation: Attraction occurs for same-direction currents; opposite directions (cross vs dot) cause repulsion.

distractors.answer: No force exists because the currents are perpendicular to each other
distractors.explanation: Both currents are perpendicular to the page; they are parallel to each other, not perpendicular.

distractors.answer: The force depends on which wire is drawn on the left side
distractors.explanation: The force depends on current directions, not the position of the wires in the diagram.

toLevel4.question: A uniform magnetic field is directed at 45° into the page. How would this be represented in a diagram?
toLevel4.correct: Crosses combined with arrows showing the horizontal component along the page surface
toLevel4.correctExplanation: A field at 45° has both an into-page component (crosses) and a component along the page surface (shown by arrows), requiring a combination.

distractors.answer: Dots rotated at 45° to indicate the tilted field angle
distractors.explanation: Dots and crosses represent only the perpendicular component; rotation is not meaningful for these symbols.

distractors.answer: Standard crosses alone since any non-zero into-page component uses crosses
distractors.explanation: Crosses alone would miss the in-plane component; a 45° field requires both representations.

distractors.answer: Half-filled circles to indicate the field is partially into the page
distractors.explanation: Half-filled circles are not a standard convention; the combination of crosses and arrows is correct.

toLevel4.question: In an exam question, a region is shown with evenly spaced crosses. A wire carrying 2.0 A runs horizontally through this region. What additional information do you need to calculate the force on the wire?
toLevel4.correct: The magnetic field strength (B) and the length of wire in the field region (l)
toLevel4.correctExplanation: With current and direction known, F = nIlB requires B and l. The crosses confirm the field is perpendicular to the current.

distractors.answer: Only the speed at which the wire is moving through the field
distractors.explanation: The wire is a conductor with current, not a moving charge; speed of the wire is not in F = nIlB.

distractors.answer: The temperature of the wire and the surrounding air pressure
distractors.explanation: Temperature and pressure do not appear in the force formula F = nIlB.

distractors.answer: The mass of the wire and the gravitational field strength there
distractors.explanation: Mass and gravity are needed for the weight of the wire, not the magnetic force on it.

toLevel4.question: A student's diagram shows dots on both sides of a wire carrying current upward. The dots are more densely packed on the left side. What does this density difference represent?
toLevel4.correct: The magnetic field is stronger on the left side than on the right side
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Higher symbol density indicates a stronger field, just as closer field lines indicate stronger fields in line diagrams.

distractors.answer: The field reverses direction between the left and right sides
distractors.explanation: Both sides show dots, meaning the field comes out of the page on both sides; density shows strength difference.

distractors.answer: The diagram has a drawing error because dots must be evenly distributed
distractors.explanation: Uneven distribution is intentional, representing a non-uniform field that is stronger on one side.

distractors.answer: The left side has a field but the right side does not have any field
distractors.explanation: Both sides have dots indicating a field; the right side simply has a weaker field.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about applying the right-hand slap rule with the convention.
toLevel4.sentence: For a current flowing upward through a field of crosses, the right-hand slap rule gives a force directed to the {{blank:1}}.

1.correctExplanation: Thumb up (current), fingers into page (crosses), palm faces left — so the force on the wire is to the left.

distractors.answer: right
distractors.explanation: Right would be the result if the field were out of the page (dots); with crosses, the force is to the left.

distractors.answer: top
distractors.explanation: The force is perpendicular to both current and field, in the plane of the page, not upward.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about current direction convention.
toLevel4.sentence: A wire carrying current out of the page is shown by a {{blank:1}} at the wire's cross-section in the diagram.

1.correctExplanation: Current out of the page is shown by a dot, using the same convention as for magnetic field direction.

distractors.answer: cross
distractors.explanation: A cross would indicate current going into the page, not out of it.

distractors.answer: square
distractors.explanation: A square is not part of the standard dot-cross convention.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about force on an electron.
toLevel4.sentence: Because the electron has a {{blank:1}} charge, the force on it is {{blank:2}} to the direction given by the right-hand slap rule.

1.correctExplanation: The electron carries a negative charge of -1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

distractors.answer: positive
distractors.explanation: The electron has a negative charge; positive charges follow the right-hand rule directly.

distractors.answer: neutral
distractors.explanation: A neutral particle would experience no magnetic force; the electron is negatively charged.

2.correctExplanation: The right-hand slap rule gives the force direction for positive charges; for negative charges like electrons, the force is reversed.

distractors.answer: identical
distractors.explanation: The force direction for negative charges is opposite to the right-hand rule result, not identical.

distractors.answer: perpendicular
distractors.explanation: The force is reversed (180°), not at 90° to the right-hand rule result.

toLevel5.question: A problem involves a proton moving at an angle of 30° to a magnetic field directed into the page. How should the arrow convention be combined with vector analysis to solve this problem?
toLevel5.correct: Decompose the velocity into components parallel and perpendicular to B; only the perpendicular component produces a force
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The crosses show B is into the page. The velocity component along B produces no force; only the perpendicular component contributes to F = qv⊥B.

distractors.answer: Use the full velocity in F = qvB because the angle does not affect the result
distractors.explanation: The force depends on the perpendicular component of velocity; using full v overestimates the force.

distractors.answer: The problem cannot be solved because the convention only works for 90° angles
distractors.explanation: The convention works for any angle; vector decomposition handles non-perpendicular cases.

distractors.answer: Ignore the crosses and treat the problem as if no field exists at that angle
distractors.explanation: The field exists at all angles; the perpendicular component still produces a force.

toLevel5.question: In a cathode ray tube, electrons are deflected by a magnetic field. The field is shown as crosses in the diagram. An engineer wants to deflect the beam upward instead of downward. What change is needed?
toLevel5.correct: Reverse the field direction from into the page (crosses) to out of the page (dots)
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Reversing the field direction reverses the force direction on the electrons, changing the deflection from downward to upward.

distractors.answer: Increase the number of crosses drawn in the diagram region shown
distractors.explanation: More crosses would increase the field strength and force magnitude, but not change its direction.

distractors.answer: Move the crosses to a different position on the page surface instead
distractors.explanation: Moving symbols changes where the field is, not its direction; reversing direction requires changing to dots.

distractors.answer: Replace the crosses with horizontal arrows pointing to the right side
distractors.explanation: Horizontal arrows would represent a different field orientation, not necessarily achieving the desired deflection.

toLevel5.question: A complex diagram shows a region with crosses transitioning to dots across a boundary line. What physical scenario could this represent?
toLevel5.correct: A magnetic field that reverses direction from into the page to out of the page across the boundary
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The transition from crosses to dots indicates the field flips direction at the boundary, which occurs in some electromagnetic configurations.

distractors.answer: A field that gets weaker across the boundary but maintains its direction
distractors.explanation: Weakening would be shown by sparser symbols of the same type, not a change from crosses to dots.

distractors.answer: A region where no magnetic field exists at the boundary line itself
distractors.explanation: At the boundary where the field reverses, it passes through zero, but the diagram shows field on both sides.

distractors.answer: An error in the diagram because crosses and dots cannot appear together
distractors.explanation: Both can appear in different regions of the same diagram; they simply show different field directions.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the limitations of the dot-cross convention when representing complex three-dimensional field configurations.
toLevel5.correct: The convention can only show the perpendicular-to-page component and must be supplemented with arrows for in-plane components
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Fields at arbitrary angles have both in-plane and perpendicular components; the dot-cross convention handles only the perpendicular part.

distractors.answer: The convention has no limitations and can represent any field configuration fully
distractors.explanation: The convention can only show one component of the field; arbitrary 3D fields need additional representation.

distractors.answer: The convention only works for uniform fields and fails for non-uniform fields
distractors.explanation: The convention works for both uniform and non-uniform fields by varying symbol density.

distractors.answer: The convention cannot be used together with field line diagrams at all
distractors.explanation: Dots, crosses, and field lines can be combined in the same diagram to show full 3D information.

toLevel5.question: A student solving a problem gets a force pointing into the page. How should they represent this force in their solution diagram?
toLevel5.correct: Use a cross at the point where the force acts to show it is directed into the page
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The dot-cross convention applies to any vector, including force. A cross at the application point shows the force direction into the page.

distractors.answer: Draw an arrow pointing downward because into the page means downward always
distractors.explanation: Into the page is a distinct direction from downward; it is perpendicular to the page surface.

distractors.answer: Forces cannot be shown using the dot and cross convention at all
distractors.explanation: The convention can represent any vector direction perpendicular to the page, including force.

distractors.answer: Use a dot because forces always point in the opposite direction to the field
distractors.explanation: The force direction depends on the specific problem; it is not always opposite to the field.

toLevel5.question: How would a rotating magnetic field (one that changes direction over time) be represented using the arrow convention in a sequence of diagrams?
toLevel5.correct: A series of frames showing the symbols changing from dots to arrows to crosses as the field rotates
toLevel5.correctExplanation: As the field rotates through 360°, its perpendicular component changes from out-of-page (dots) through in-plane (arrows) to into-page (crosses) and back.

distractors.answer: A single diagram with both dots and crosses is sufficient for any rotating field
distractors.explanation: A single frame cannot show time evolution; a sequence is needed to show the changing direction.

distractors.answer: Rotating fields cannot be represented using the arrow convention at all
distractors.explanation: A sequence of diagrams can represent a rotating field by showing different snapshots in time.

distractors.answer: The symbols themselves would need to be drawn rotating on the page surface
distractors.explanation: Individual dots and crosses do not rotate; the convention changes between symbols as the field direction changes.

toLevel5.question: In Thomson's experiment to measure the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron, both electric and magnetic fields were applied. The magnetic field was shown as crosses. Why was it essential that Thomson knew the exact direction of the field?
toLevel5.correct: The deflection direction depends on the field direction, which was needed to determine the sign and trajectory of the particles
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Thomson used the known field direction to predict deflection and identify the charge sign of the cathode rays as negative.

distractors.answer: The direction did not matter because only the field magnitude affected the result
distractors.explanation: Direction was critical for predicting deflection direction and determining the charge sign.

distractors.answer: Thomson needed to know the direction only to draw a prettier diagram of results
distractors.explanation: The direction was essential physics, not aesthetics; it determined which way the beam deflected.

distractors.answer: The direction was needed to ensure the crosses looked correct in his published papers
distractors.explanation: The crosses represented real physical field direction that determined experimental outcomes.

toLevel5.question: A physics simulation uses vectors at grid points to represent a magnetic field. Compared to the dot-cross convention, what advantage does this computational approach have?
toLevel5.correct: Vectors show exact magnitude and arbitrary direction, not just into/out of page
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Computational vector fields can represent any direction and precise magnitude at every point, while dots and crosses only show the perpendicular-to-page component.

distractors.answer: Vectors are always less accurate than dots and crosses for field representation
distractors.explanation: Vectors provide more information; dots and crosses are a simplified convention for 2D diagrams.

distractors.answer: The dot-cross convention contains more information than a full vector description
distractors.explanation: A full vector at each point contains more information than the binary in/out representation.

distractors.answer: Both methods are identical in the information they convey about the field
distractors.explanation: Vectors convey full 3D direction and precise magnitude; dots and crosses are limited to one component.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about the convention's limitations.
toLevel5.sentence: The dot-cross convention can only represent the {{blank:1}} of the field that is perpendicular to the page; in-plane components require separate arrows.

1.correctExplanation: A vector field at an angle to the page has both a perpendicular component (shown by dots/crosses) and an in-plane component (shown by arrows).

distractors.answer: entirety
distractors.explanation: The convention does not show the entire field vector, only the perpendicular component.

distractors.answer: absence
distractors.explanation: The convention shows the presence and direction of the perpendicular component, not its absence.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the sentence about Thomson's experiment.
toLevel5.sentence: Thomson used the known {{blank:1}} of the magnetic field (shown as crosses) to predict the deflection direction and confirm that cathode rays carry {{blank:2}} charge.

1.correctExplanation: Knowing the field direction allowed Thomson to predict which way the beam should deflect for positive versus negative charge.

distractors.answer: temperature
distractors.explanation: Temperature is irrelevant to beam deflection; field direction determines the force on charged particles.

distractors.answer: colour
distractors.explanation: Magnetic fields have no colour; it is the direction that determines deflection.

2.correctExplanation: The beam deflected in the direction expected for negative charges, confirming electrons carry negative charge.

distractors.answer: positive
distractors.explanation: Thomson's experiment showed cathode rays deflect as negative charges, not positive.

distractors.answer: neutral
distractors.explanation: Neutral particles would not be deflected by a magnetic field; the beam was deflected, confirming charge.
